items.headline: Druze: Sunday's Route 6 protest followed the stabbing of a young Druze man from Isfiya in Jaffa; his father says it was for speaking Arabic, police say it began as an argument
items.lead: Three young Druze men from Isfiya were attacked on Kibbutz Galuyot Street in Jaffa on the night of 24–25 October; one, aged 18, was stabbed and taken to Ichilov hospital with moderate injuries.
items.text: His father says the three were attacked because they were speaking Arabic, and Kan called it a "racist attack". Police say it began as an argument; three suspects aged 18 and 19 were arrested and two knives seized, and no racist motive was mentioned at the remand hearing (Ynet; Mako). This is the cause of Sunday afternoon's protest that closed Route 6 at the Elyakim interchange, which the 25 October edition could not yet explain: about 100 Druze protesters burned tires and blocked the road for about an hour, and police arrested four (Ynet; i24NEWS). The motive is disputed and not yet established.

sources.name: Map: Kibbutz Galuyot Street, Jaffa (approximate) (Google Maps)

items.headline: Sweida (Syria): Israeli Druze figures and experts condemn US envoy Barrack's claim tying the Druze area to captagon drug production
items.lead: Druze diplomat and historian Reda Mansour called the remarks "highly irresponsible", saying they "put the vulnerable Druze community in southern Syria at direct risk of sectarian violence".
items.text: Barrack's remarks and Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri's rejection of them were reported in the 25 October edition. US envoy Tom Barrack also said "Israel and Syria will come to terms" (Middle East Eye). In the Jerusalem Post on 25 October, Mordechai Kedar of the Begin-Sadat Center said Barrack's "lack of understanding" has "brought a lot of damage to the whole Middle East", and Jonathan Hessen of the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security called the remarks "dismaying" and without factual basis, noting that Jordan's air strikes in southern Syria mostly hit Daraa province, where Bedouin live, not Sweida. Captagon is an illegal amphetamine-type pill made largely in Syria. The Jerusalem Post notes the UN figure of more than 1,300 Druze killed in the July 2025 Sweida massacres. No reaction from the Israeli government was found.

items.headline: EU security mission for Lebanon: Ireland's defense minister wants Irish troops in it for both peacekeeping and peace enforcement
items.lead: Helen McEntee told RTÉ's This Week on 25 October that Irish troops should be able to take part in "both"; this needs a change to Ireland's "Triple Lock" rule, which she wants passed by the end of the year.
items.text: The Triple Lock requires government approval, Dáil approval and a UN mandate before more than 12 Irish troops are deployed abroad. McEntee also described villages in southern Lebanon destroyed "at the hands of the IDF" (RTÉ). No Israeli reaction to the EU mission or to Ireland's plans was found this morning.

items.headline: Le Pen launches her campaign in Orléans: a "national union" government led by Bardella and France as "a nation of peace"; Jewish student activists interrupt Bardella
items.lead: Speaking to more than 8,000 people at the RN congress on Sunday, Marine Le Pen promised a "pluralist" government of "national union" with Jordan Bardella as its "conductor".
items.text: She said France must be "une nation de paix" and that she does not want young people "to die in war adventures" (franceinfo). Le Monde describes a speech between "radicalism" and "optimism" in a city under heavy police guard. Activists of the Union of Jewish Students of France interrupted Bardella's speech and were roughly removed (franceinfo). The Interior Ministry's final count for the 24 October marches is 1,314 arrests, up from nearly 1,000 reported that evening (Le Monde). Polymarket (read 4:30 a.m. Israel time, 26 October; about 157 million dollars traded): Le Pen 43.25 percent (down 2.5 in a day), Philippe 15.5, Lisnard 14.05, Mélenchon 10.5, Glucksmann 4.75, Hollande 3.15, Retailleau 1.35.

items.headline: Trenton Ironhawks win their first home game 4–1 before 7,032 fans, the city's first professional hockey in 13 years
items.lead: The privately owned ECHL team beat the Adirondack Thunder at CURE Insurance Arena on Saturday night, 24 October.
items.text: Mikey Colella scored the first Ironhawks home goal 15:43 into the first period, and goaltender Fanti made 28 saves (team report). Trenton had had no professional hockey since the Trenton Titans folded in 2013. The next home game is Wednesday against Reading.

items.headline: Trump tells a Georgia rally that Denmark "gave us Greenland"; the 22 October US-Danish agreement does not cover Greenland
items.lead: At a rally in Perry, Georgia, on 24 October Trump said Denmark "gave us Greenland", which is false.
items.text: The memorandum of understanding signed on 22 October "does not apply to Greenland or the Faroe Islands" (Tribune India, which also fact-checks his claim that the US "got" Venezuela). Norwegian outlets also reported the claim (seen in news-search headlines only, not opened).

items.headline: Kremlin: Russia, China and the US are "in principle ready" for a Putin–Xi–Trump summit at the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, 18–19 November
items.lead: Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said "preparations have already begun" for a three-way meeting on the sidelines of APEC.
items.text: This is the Kremlin's account (Anadolu Agency); I found no confirmation of a three-way meeting from Beijing or Washington.

items.headline: Scotland: new Norstat poll puts Yes to independence at 52 percent; 47 percent want a second referendum within five years
items.lead: Norstat for The Sunday Times surveyed 1,000 Scottish voters on 20–23 October; Yes leads 52 to 48 when undecided voters are excluded, and 47 percent want a referendum within five years against 42 percent opposed.
items.text: First Minister John Swinney's net rating is minus 17 (24 percent good, 41 bad), which polling expert Sir John Curtice calls a new low. Prime Minister Andy Burnham's is minus 5 (29 good, 34 bad). Westminster voting intention: SNP 32 percent, Labour 21. New Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra is unknown to most: 41 percent said "don't know". SNP deputy leader Keith Brown says this is the sixth poll with a Yes lead since Burnham became prime minister (The National).

items.headline: Musk: SpaceX has closed a 40-billion-dollar financing, mostly callable debt, to pay for AI chips arriving in early 2027
items.lead: Musk posted on X on Sunday that the money is for GPUs (AI processors) due in the first half of 2027.
items.text: Bloomberg had reported that Goldman Sachs was leading talks with investors including Apollo, through a separate company (a special purpose vehicle) that keeps the debt off SpaceX's balance sheet (CNBC, citing Bloomberg). CNBC says SpaceX's "Super Intelligence" unit, which includes xAI, had third-quarter revenue of 7.56 billion dollars, up from 813 million. Musk predicts that more than 200 "neocloud" companies (firms that rent out AI computing) will fail or merge. Grok Bot's changelog is still at version 0.75.5 (23 October), and Cursor's changelog has nothing newer than 16 October.

items.headline: Starship: SpaceX fires all 33 engines of Super Heavy Booster 22 for about 15 seconds
items.lead: The static fire test on 25 October in Texas ended with throttle changes that imitated a landing burn.
items.text: Booster 22 is expected to fly on Flight 15, planned for November with an attempt to catch the booster; SpaceX still needs a new FAA license for that flight (iXBT, Russian). The FAA's planning slides of 22 October still show Flight 15 no earlier than 8 November (25 October edition).

items.headline: Michael Downs begins a four-week online seminar on Land's Xenosystems on 1 November; Net Void shares it
items.lead: Michael Downs (@JutlandGhost), author of The Dangerous Maybe blog and the essay "Capital vs. Timenergy: A Zizekian Critique of Nick Land", posted on 24 October that his course on Xenosystems starts on 1 November; Net Void reposted it the next morning.
items.text: The course is the second month of Philosophy Portal's paid "Theory Fiction and Politics" series (150 Canadian dollars, with recordings). Its four Sunday sessions are Neoreaction (1 November), Artificial Intelligence (8 November), Time (15 November) and Horrorism (22 November), each listed at 8:30 p.m. Central European time (9:30 p.m. Israel time). The page calls Xenosystems "a foundational book of extreme political philosophy often referred to as the neoreactionary movement". Also on Net Void's list: a repost of patallax's "vibe numogramming" post. Land himself (@xenocosmography) posted only on politics since the last check, nothing on cyphers, gematria or Gnostic Calvinism.

items.headline: Netanyahu names Colombia as a country Israel "brought back" with "countermeasures" against sanctions
items.lead: In a Channel 14 interview on Saturday 24 October, Netanyahu said Israel had blocked every attempt to sanction it "with countermeasures", citing Colombia and Slovenia.
items.text: He gave the example of Britain ("we closed their consulate in Jerusalem") and of "bringing back countries that had moved away, like Colombia or Slovenia" (Europa Press). In Colombia, Gustavo Petro's Historic Pact lost the May–June election to Abelardo de la Espriella; in Slovenia, a right-wing coalition led by Janez Janša's SDS took over after the March election. Europa Press and several Latin American outlets read the remark as a hint of Israeli involvement in those changes of government; Netanyahu did not say what the countermeasures were. No Colombian government reaction was found.

items.headline: Shamir Energy takes a 10-year option to build a 100-megawatt data center at Ashdot Ya'akov in the Jordan Valley, with its own power plant or storage
items.lead: Shamir Energy, 72 percent owned by Mivtach Shamir, signed for an exclusive option on part of about 106 dunams (about 26 acres) in the Kinneret industrial park at Kibbutz Ashdot Ya'akov Meuhad, Yesodot Eitanim announced on 23 October.
items.text: A small power station or energy-storage site is planned next to the data center to supply its electricity, at a time when the Electricity Authority plans to allow only about 1,000 megawatts of new data center load against requests of about 27,000 megawatts (Calcalist). The option requires feasibility studies, permits and financing; if used, the land lease runs almost 25 years, and the industrial park may take up to 18 percent of the operating company. Calcalist says this may mark the entry of energy companies into a field so far led by real estate firms such as Azrieli, Mega Or and Melisron.

items.headline: Land posts a Strauss–Howe thread on X: a 'secular-religious lodestone' for each 'Turning,' with the Great Replacement as the fourth and 'the exemplary crime of the dawning aeon'
items.lead: At about 4:25 AM Israel time on 26 October, Nick Land (@xenocosmography) posted a list that assigns one 'secular-religious lodestone' to each of the four Turnings of the Strauss–Howe generational theory, then added three replies within 25 minutes. It extends the 'Fourth Turning' framing of his four-step plan in the 23 October item.
items.text: The post reads: "Secular-religious lodestone after each Strauss and Howe 'Turning' / First (~1787-1866) Nonrepresentative (colonial) government / Second (~1867-1946) African Slavery / Third (~1947-2026) The Holocaust / Fourth (~2027-) The Great Replacement." He edited it: the first version, at about 3:46 AM, gave the first period as "~1777-1866". In replies on the same thread he wrote: "The Great Replacement is the exemplary crime of the dawning aeon, with all our heroes and villains to be defined by it" (about 4:32 AM); "Whatever you do to promote the Great Replacement will be immortalized in infamy, and whatever you do to reverse it will be blessed by posterity" (about 4:38 AM); and "A Joe Biden, Boris Johnson, or Angela Merkel is no less emblematic of definitive historical criminality to the new generation than a Joseph Goebbels or Adolf Eichmann was to the last" (about 4:50 AM). The main post had about 18,600 views as of about 3 PM Israel time. The 'Great Replacement' is a far-right theory that Western elites are deliberately replacing native populations through immigration; Land presents it here as a crime that will define the coming era, and I did not verify the claim itself. These are his own statements, quoted from X. I read the posts through the X API and checked the wording against the fxtwitter mirror of X; both show the same X posts, and I found no outside coverage of the thread. Also since this morning's edition: Net Void (@Net__Void) reposted patallax's 'what 14 years of Atlantean Music of the Spheres classes does to a mf'er' and posted 'Malfoid casts a gematria spell' (about 10:35 AM, with an attached link I could not identify). I found nothing new from Land on the KJV, Gnostic Calvinism or numerology, and no new Land interview or talk. Cyphers' scheduled streams (Doomer vs Accelerationism on 7 November, then Thelema on 8 November, Book of Paths and Memetic Magick on 14 November, and Gnosticism on 21 November) are unchanged from the earlier items.

items.headline: Israel votes today: 7.33 million eligible voters, 12,018 polling stations and 36 lists; polls open 7 a.m. to 10 p.m.
items.lead: Israelis elect the 26th Knesset today, Tuesday, 27 October.
items.text: Ynet reports 7,331,981 eligible voters, 12,018 polling stations and 36 party lists. Polls are open from 7:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m.; in small towns, hospitals, prisons and nursing homes they close at 8:00 p.m. There are about 250 polling stations in hospitals, and special stations for residents still displaced from Be'eri ([map](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=31.4242,34.4911)), Kfar Aza ([map](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=31.4833,34.5333)), Nir Oz ([map](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=31.3096,34.4008)) and Holit ([map](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=31.2319,34.3265)). These figures come from Ynet only and are unconfirmed by a second source. (Map coordinates: OpenStreetMap.)

items.headline: Netanyahu–Zamir clash: TV report says the IDF chief alone opposed a pre-election move against Iran; Netanyahu says he does not plan to fire him
items.lead: Reports on Monday said Netanyahu and IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir clashed over the timing of a preparatory action against Iran and over the Hebron operation.
items.text: According to Ynet, the disputes peaked at a meeting on Sunday at the Palmachim base ([map, approximate](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=31.8991,34.6913)). Netanyahu, Defense Minister Katz, Mossad chief Roman Gofman and Shin Bet chief David Zini backed the action; Zamir feared a miscalculation that could bring an Iranian strike on Israel. Officials quoted by Ynet expect Zamir to be out if Netanyahu wins. Netanyahu's office called the report "total fake news", and Katz called it "an invention and a complete lie". The Times of Israel's summary of the Israeli TV report says Zamir was the only security chief opposed. Haaretz's headline, from a CNN report, says Zamir warned his American counterpart that striking Iran would disrupt Israel's election; Katz denied any intention to strike before the vote. Late Monday Maariv carried Netanyahu's statement: "I do not intend to fire the chief of staff, and we will keep working together for Israel's security." (The Times of Israel and Haaretz articles were not readable; only their feed summaries were.)

items.headline: Last day of the campaign: Netanyahu at the Western Wall, Eisenkot on a Tel Aviv bar tour, Bennett in three cities
items.lead: The leaders spent Monday, the last day before the vote, on final appearances.
items.text: Netanyahu prayed at the Western Wall ([map](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=31.7767,35.2344)); Ynet reports that his note read "Netzach Yisrael lo yeshaker" ("The Eternal One of Israel will not lie"). Gadi Eisenkot made a bar tour in Tel Aviv ([map](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=32.0853,34.7818)) and met friends from his old Golani unit; the Yashar campaign projected "offices for rent" onto the Likud building. Naftali Bennett campaigned in Be'er Sheva ([map](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=31.2457,34.7925)), Givatayim ([map](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=32.073,34.8113)) and Herzliya ([map](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=32.1656,34.8469)) and will vote in Ra'anana ([map](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=32.186,34.8678)). Yair Golan attacked the Yashar "big party" campaign. (Ynet; map coordinates: OpenStreetMap.)

items.headline: Trump denies Netanyahu asked for his endorsement; Netanyahu met the police chief despite the election committee's ban; Likud to film Arab voters
items.lead: Trump said on Monday that he "never spoke about it" with Netanyahu, contradicting US officials and an Axios report.
items.text: Boarding Air Force One for Mississippi on 26 October, Trump said: "I never spoke about it… I put out both endorsements." US officials quoted by the Jerusalem Post, and an Axios report, said Netanyahu had called twice in three days and suggested wording; Likud denies it (Jerusalem Post). Netanyahu met Police Commissioner Daniel Levy and National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir and raised concern that "left-wing anarchists" could disrupt the vote, though the Central Election Committee had barred such talks (Times of Israel and Haaretz feed summaries). Haaretz reports that Likud has spent millions of shekels on teams to film Arab voters near polling stations and that Netanyahu is weighing a "rigged election" campaign if he loses (Haaretz, first paragraphs). The Sydney Morning Herald reported, via the Times of Israel and Haaretz, that the Australian billionaire James Packer, a witness in Netanyahu's trial, paid the firm of Netanyahu's lawyer 1.25 million dollars, 50,000 dollars a month for two years; Packer says the payments were unrelated to the trial (feed summaries only; unconfirmed).

items.headline: Polymarket on voting morning: Eisenkot 54.9 percent to be prime minister, Netanyahu 27.5
items.lead: Bettors moved further toward Eisenkot overnight.
items.text: At about 4:18 a.m. Israel time on 27 October, Polymarket's next-prime-minister market (about 56.7 million dollars traded) had Gadi Eisenkot at 54.85 percent (up 4.45 points from the previous morning), Netanyahu 27.5 (up 2), Bennett 9.5 (down 3) and Lieberman 2.05. In the most-seats market (about 4.08 million dollars traded), Yashar was at 68.5 percent (down 1) and Likud at 31.

sources.name: Polymarket: Prime Minister of Israel after the next election

items.headline: Sweida (Syria): Jordanian air strikes after the Karak church attack hit Shahba; Syria says 7 dead and closes the Nassib crossing
items.lead: Jordan struck what it called militant hideouts in southern Syria, in Daraa and Sweida provinces, after Friday's gun attack on a church funeral in Karak governorate.
items.text: The 23 October attack on a Greek Orthodox funeral in the village of Hamoud killed 9 people and wounded at least 34; three suspects, two brothers and a brother-in-law, were arrested after a shootout in al-Judayyda (Al Jazeera; Reuters via Al-Monitor). Syrian Civil Defense said four sites were hit in Daraa and Sweida provinces and seven people were killed, including three children and a woman; one strike hit a residential building in Shahba, in Sweida province, killing a 60-year-old man, and five members of one family died in a tent in Al-Tai, Daraa (Al Jazeera). The Times of Israel's live blog headline later put the toll at 8. Syria denies Jordan's claim that the strikes were coordinated with Damascus and closed the Nassib crossing, Jordan's only open crossing with Syria (Al Jazeera; Al-Monitor).

items.headline: Reuters: Hezbollah is preparing for a new war with Israel, with tens of millions of dollars from Iran
items.lead: Sources told Reuters that Hezbollah is rearming and rebuilding its command structure, though it is not yet fully ready.
items.text: According to the report, Hezbollah has received tens of millions of dollars from Iran on top of about 200 million dollars for displaced families. It is buying explosives, making attack drones and rebuilding command structures lost in fighting at Bint Jbeil and on the Ali al-Taher ridge. The US State Department said it would keep squeezing Hezbollah's finances. Haaretz carried the same report (headline). EUSM watch: nothing new on the planned EU mission in Lebanon since 26 October.

items.headline: Bolsonaro's party accepts Lula's win; Moraes bars Flávio Bolsonaro from leaving Brazil; Trump calls the vote extension "very strange"
items.lead: The Liberal Party (PL) said it recognizes the result, while Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered Flávio to hand over his passports.
items.text: PL president Valdemar Costa Neto said in a note: "Reconhecemos o resultado presidencial, proclamado pelo TSE" ("We recognize the presidential result proclaimed by the electoral court"), while still questioning social spending before the vote. The final count gave Lula 64.2 million votes (51.7 percent) and Flávio 59.8 million (48.2 percent) (Agência Brasil). Moraes barred Flávio from leaving the country and ordered him to surrender his passports in the inquiry involving lawyer Willer Tomaz and Alcazar Holdings (Madeira); the decision cites a remark by his brother Eduardo that Flávio should leave the country if he lost (Agência Brasil). Trump said: "I like Lula… a very bad look… The extension given was very strange" (Jerusalem Post); Ynet quotes him calling it "another rigged election". Justice Cristiano Zanin had extended voting by two hours at the Workers' Party's request; both campaigns had asked for an extension.

items.headline: Cluster17 for Politico: Mélenchon second at 18.5 percent, Philippe falls to 16; Polymarket has Philippe back up to 18.5
items.lead: A new Cluster17 poll (19–22 October, 3,000 people, online, published 26 October) puts Philippe third behind Le Pen and Mélenchon.
items.text: With Philippe as the centrist candidate: Le Pen 33 (up 2), Mélenchon 18.5 (down 0.5), Philippe 16 (down 3), Glucksmann 13 (up 1), Retailleau 8 (up 0.5), Zemmour 4, Dupont-Aignan 3, Roussel 2, Tondelier 2, Arthaud 0.5. With Lisnard tested: Lisnard 8, Le Pen 30.5, Retailleau 7, Zemmour 3.5. With Attal instead of Philippe: Attal 12, Mélenchon 19.5, Glucksmann 14. Only 49 percent of Macron's 2022 voters back Philippe; 29 percent back Glucksmann (Cluster17 report; Politico). Polymarket at about 4:18 a.m. Israel time on 27 October (about 157.5 million dollars traded): Le Pen 43.65, Philippe 18.5 (up 3 since the previous morning), Lisnard 13.65, Mélenchon 10.5, Glucksmann 3.35, Hollande 3.25.

items.headline: St-Pierre Plamondon will meet Macron in France "in the coming weeks" after a phone call
items.lead: Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said on Monday evening that he spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron by phone and that they agreed to meet in France.
items.text: In a post on X, the premier said he expressed Quebec's support and solidarity and condemned "troubles fomented by the ultra-left" in France. They discussed closer economic ties and new cooperation on digital sovereignty, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence, the 20th Francophonie Summit next month in Phnom Penh, and the election of the next secretary general of the International Organization of La Francophonie. No date for the meeting has been set (TVA Nouvelles, quoting his post).

items.headline: "Strangers" is a finalist for Barnes & Noble's 2026 Book of the Year
items.lead: Belle Burden's "Strangers: A Memoir of Marriage" is one of 16 finalists chosen by Barnes & Noble booksellers.
items.text: Barnes & Noble announced the finalists on 22 October; the list has six novels, seven nonfiction books and three books for children and young adults. Booksellers vote, and the winner will be announced on 12 November. Other finalists include Patrick Radden Keefe's "London Falling", Barbara Kingsolver's "Partita" and Colson Whitehead's "Cool Machine" (Barnes & Noble press release).

items.headline: Anthropic's IPO filing: up to 120.5 billion dollars for SpaceX computing power through 2029
items.lead: Anthropic's public S-1 filing, dated 26 October, discloses agreements to spend up to 120.5 billion dollars on SpaceX computing capacity.
items.text: Monthly payments would rise to about 3.1 billion dollars once all contracted capacity is delivered, which Anthropic expects in December 2026. The amount is a maximum: the first fixed periods end in January and March 2027, and after that either side can end the deal on 90 days' notice. Reuters had reported 84.5 billion dollars from the confidential version in September. Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. SpaceX's third-quarter revenue was 14.575 billion dollars, including 7.56 billion from its Super Intelligence segment (Yahoo Finance; TeslaNorth). Barron's described the deal in a headline; the Barron's article was not opened.

items.headline: Grok Bot 0.75.8: Bots can propose changes to Auto-review rules, fewer approval cards, and connector fixes; Cursor launches an Agent SDK
items.lead: The Grok Bot changelog shows version 0.75.8 (24 October), which also covers 0.75.6 and 0.75.7; the last version reported here was 0.75.5.
items.text: New: in the app, a Bot can offer to add, change or remove one of your Auto-review rules on a card you confirm. Improved: Auto-review takes a second look before showing an approval card; saving or editing a routine no longer counts as risky by itself; scheduling uses whichever calendar is connected (Google or Outlook); in a private chat a Bot reads your own private files without asking; Team Bots are closed to people not on their share list. Fixed: Bots can use new tools or fields a connector such as X adds without reconnecting; expired connectors show "Authenticate"; Slack posts from routines no longer notify your phone (Grok Bot changelog). Cursor's changelog has a 20 October entry: the Agent SDK, which defines an agent as a folder of code (instructions, tools, skills, MCP connections, channels), tests it with evals and deploys it to Cursor or your own servers; agents can wake on GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket events, Slack mentions, webhooks or a schedule (Cursor changelog).

items.headline: The Based Atlantis calculator is by @patallax: an ES−AQ gematria calculator with a Numogram view
items.lead: The Based Atlantis page noted here on 25 October now has a known author.
items.text: The site's main page is a gematria calculator that computes ES minus AQ values and has a Numogram feature, and it is signed "vibecoded by @patallax" (Based Atlantis). Patallax announced it on X on 24 October at 10:02 p.m. Israel time; the post had about 7,360 views, 239 likes and 192 bookmarks when checked. Other activity on the watch list: Doomcrypt posted "Money Is the Original Hyperstition = 666"; Net Void posted "Malfoid casts a cyphers spell"; @AOElection posted on Original Sin; CyphersNews quoted the @IAMIRONMAN7 song "Noumenal Wolves"; @resonatingloop pushed a new GitHub repository, "hmmarium", on 24 October. Land posted only on politics; Retrochronic is unchanged (v1.0.176, 199 sources), and no new Land video or podcast appeared after the Rabbit Hole episode of 23 October.

items.headline: Andreessen publishes a new essay on AI agents and the "self-driving company"
items.lead: On 26 October 2026, Marc Andreessen published an essay titled "Let Chaos Reign, and Then Rein In Chaos" on the a16z newsletter site and as an X article on @pmarca.
items.text: On 26 October 2026, Marc Andreessen published an essay titled "Let Chaos Reign, and Then Rein In Chaos" (subtitle "Replit and the dawn of the self-driving company") on the a16z newsletter site, and posted it as an X article from @pmarca at 16:08 UTC (18:08 Israel time). It was written for the launch of Replit for Business, a product of the a16z portfolio company Replit. He argues that important workplace technologies such as the personal computer, the spreadsheet and email first arrived in a disorderly way, and that companies then had to build controlled settings that kept employee initiative alive. He says AI agents are following the same path, and that companies will become "self-driving" when people set goals and agents carry out the work. It is his first written essay found since "Investing in Cognition" on 9 September 2026, and his first original X post found since 18 October. His X posting is still far below his pre-July level: his total post count rose by 4 in the day to 27 October, and he made 47 posts in the seven days to 27 October (about 7 a day), compared with about 25 a day before July.

items.headline: Israel votes with 77.7 percent turnout, the highest since 1999; exit polls show no 61-seat majority, and overnight updates moved toward Netanyahu
items.lead: Turnout was 77.7 percent (5,695,682 of 7,331,981 eligible voters), the highest since 1999, and none of the 10 p.m. exit polls gave either bloc the 61 seats needed to govern.
items.text: At 10 p.m., Channel 12, Channel 13 and Kan all had the Netanyahu bloc at 50 seats and the Eisenkot-led "change" bloc at 52, with Likud the largest party (Channel 12: Likud 24, Yashar! 22) and the Arab parties at about 17. The right-leaning channels differed: i24NEWS had 55 to 49 and Channel 14 had 60 to 43. Overnight updates moved toward Netanyahu: Kan revised to a 51–51 tie, and Channel 12 revised to Netanyahu bloc 52, Eisenkot bloc 49 and Arab parties 19, with Likud up to 27 and Yashar! down to 21. With about 21.4 percent of votes counted (1.2 million) at 4:18 a.m. Israel time, Ynet reported Likud at 23.4 percent, Yashar! 15.7 percent and B'Yachad (Bennett–Lapid) 8.5 percent, with Ra'am at 3.2 percent, just under the 3.25 percent threshold. Early counts are not representative of the final result. Arutz Sheva projected 65 seats for the current coalition from an 11.1 percent count; this is a partisan outlet's projection and is unconfirmed. On Polymarket at about 4:30 a.m. Israel time, Netanyahu was at 53.5 percent to be the next prime minister (up 26 points in a day) and Eisenkot at 22 percent (down 33 points). Official results are due by 4 November.

items.headline: Both sides claim the night: Netanyahu says the right has a "clear majority" among Jewish voters; Eisenkot says the public "decided in favor of change"
items.lead: Netanyahu told supporters in Jerusalem that Likud is the largest party and that the right-wing bloc has a "clear, decisive majority among the Jewish public," while waiting for the real results "in the next day or two."
items.text: Eisenkot told his Yashar! headquarters, "We made history," said the public had "decided in favor of change," and said it would be "a mistake to go to another election." Bennett, speaking for B'Yachad with Lapid, said "the alliance of those who serve has defeated the coalition of draft dodgers" and signaled support for Eisenkot as prime minister; Lapid said the coalition might not be broad on the first day. United Torah Judaism leader Yitzhak Goldknopf did not rule out working with Eisenkot and said the question would go to the Torah sages. Ynet reported that people close to President Trump would prefer a unity government without Itamar Ben-Gvir (unnamed sources; unconfirmed). Haredi protesters blocked Route 4 after the exit polls were published.

items.headline: Sweida (Syria): a Saudi paper says Israel and Syria came close to a direct clash last week until US and Gulf mediation on 20 October (single source)
items.lead: Al-Majalla, as reported by Channel 14, says the US and Gulf states stepped in on 20 October and reached "loose understandings" that prevented an Israel–Syria clash over Sweida.
items.text: According to the report, Damascus sent reinforcements to the lines around Sweida after hearing that Druze forces linked to Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri planned to strike government targets, which Damascus believed was meant to draw Israel in. It also says Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani has been pressing Washington and regional states to stop Israeli army operations in southern Syria. Damascus has not confirmed that war was close, and no new security agreement has been published. This rests on a single source (Al-Majalla) and is unconfirmed.

items.headline: Druze leader Walid Jumblatt answers a State Department rebuke: nobody in Lebanon was consulted on the three-way framework
items.lead: After a State Department spokesman publicly criticized him, Jumblatt said he has the right to express his opinion and that no one in Lebanon was consulted before the US–Israel–Lebanon framework was announced.
items.text: EUSM watch: no Israeli press reaction to the planned EU mission in Lebanon was found; the only new coverage is the Irish debate over sending troops (Sinn Féin criticized Minister Helen McEntee on 27 October).

items.headline: How Israel's Druze voted: Sweida pulled some toward Likud, while the Nation-State Law and crime pushed others away
items.lead: i24NEWS Arabic reports that Druze voters were split, with some backing Likud because of Israel's actions to protect the Druze of Sweida (Syria).
items.text: Others cited the Nation-State Law, the Kaminitz planning law and crime in Druze towns as reasons to vote against the government. Vote totals by town were not yet available.

items.headline: Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil for the US after his election loss; Lula calls it a "shameful act"
items.lead: Flávio Bolsonaro left Brazil for the United States, and the US said it would grant him a visa.
items.text: President Lula called the departure an "ato vergonhoso" ("shameful act"). Agência Brasil explains that the Supreme Court (STF) investigations against him continue, and that he keeps his Senate immunities until his term ends on 1 February. The day before, Justice Moraes had barred him from leaving the country (see 27 October).

items.headline: Odoxa-Mascaret poll (27 October): 74 percent say Le Pen gains most from the 17 October riots; 67 percent feel anger
items.lead: In the Odoxa-Mascaret barometer published 27 October, 74 percent named Marine Le Pen as the main political beneficiary of the 17 October violence.
items.text: Sixty-seven percent said they felt anger, and Macron's rating was 83 percent negative. Favorable ratings: Le Pen 38 percent, Bardella 37 percent and Mélenchon 32 percent. Polymarket barely moved: Le Pen 43 percent, Édouard Philippe 17.5 percent, David Lisnard 15.5 percent and Mélenchon 11.5 percent.

items.headline: Le Pen names Hérault deputy Charles Alloncle as her campaign spokesman
items.lead: Marine Le Pen named Charles Alloncle, the RN deputy for Hérault, as spokesman for her 2027 presidential campaign.
items.text: Also on 27 October: the Senate passed the "casseurs-payeurs" bill (which makes rioters pay for damage), and chambers of commerce counted more than 2,500 shops damaged in the 17 October riots.

items.headline: St-Pierre Plamondon will boycott the Canada–EU summit in Montreal, saying Ottawa censored him; Carney: "his decision to leave the chair empty"
items.lead: Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he will not attend the Canada–EU summit in Montreal on 29–30 October, accusing Ottawa of refusing to let him speak.
items.text: Prime Minister Carney replied that it was the premier's "decision to leave the chair empty." The boycott follows the premier's planned meeting with Macron (see 27 October).

items.headline: Electricity Authority's full proposal for data centers: 1,000 MW until 2035, 200 MW per site, and guarantees of up to NIS 400 million
items.lead: The Electricity Authority published its full hearing document on connecting data centers to the grid, Globes reported on the evening of 25 October.
items.text: The proposal caps each site at 200 MW and forbids splitting a site into smaller ones to get around the cap. It sets 1,000 MW in total for new data centers until 2035, plus a 300 MW reserve for data centers serving local customers. Developers would post a guarantee of NIS 0.5 million per MW when they apply (up to NIS 100 million), rising to NIS 2 million per MW (up to NIS 400 million) once approvals are in. Quotas would go first-come, first-served to those meeting the legal thresholds; plans taking more than seven years get an automatic no, and all applications are due by 1 June 2028. On-site renewable power with storage is allowed but gives no priority, and priority rules (periphery, flexibility at peak hours, efficiency) are still undecided. The authority froze new data-center connection requests in July after requests totaling 27 GW, three times Israel's entire generating capacity, came in. Public comments are open until 17 November, so the final decision will likely fall to the next government. Mega Or, which had planned more than 1,000 MW in Hadera, filed a stock-exchange report on 26 October about the hearing (seen only as an Investing.com headline).

items.headline: India and the Bibliothèque nationale de France agree to digitize Indian manuscripts held in Paris and share OCR tools for Indian scripts
items.lead: India's Ministry of Culture and the Bibliothèque nationale de France (BnF) signed a memorandum of understanding in Paris on 26 October under the Gyan Bharatam Mission.
items.text: It was signed by Vivek Aggarwal for the ministry and Gilles Pécout for the BnF. It covers five areas: digitization, sharing on India's National Digital Repository, technology exchange, conservation, and research. It includes digitizing manuscripts of Indian origin held by the BnF and exchanging "OCR/HTR tools for Indian scripts" (software that reads printed and handwritten text). Source: the Indian government's press release; the DD News copy could not be opened.

items.headline: Grok Bot 0.77.0: approval per login for 1Password, memory import from other assistants, a Permissions page and 30-minute approval cards
items.lead: xAI's changelog dated 26 October lists Grok Bot 0.77.0 (with 0.76.0), titled "Permissions, Vault payments, and question cards."
items.text: New: 1Password approval for each login; importing memory from another assistant; cards that ask several questions at once; a copy button for tables; a Vault Payments tab; address autocomplete; a Gmail sign-out notice; Portuguese (Portugal); pinned emoji; page owners can delete Pages; Order Concierge and Deal Watcher templates; custom MCP servers with a private certificate authority; and Team Bot features. Improved: a new typeface; a Permissions section in Settings that lists Auto-review rules; approval cards stay open 30 minutes instead of 10; background work started in your own words no longer needs approval; dictation that types while you speak; and bots try saved Vault logins and cards before a password manager.

items.headline: NASA draft study shows SpaceX's planned Kennedy campus: about 400 acres, 3,300 workers by 2045 and a Starship test stand
items.lead: A 239-page NASA draft environmental assessment released this month describes SpaceX's planned expansion at Roberts Road, Kennedy Space Center.
items.text: SpaceX would grow from the 167 acres it leases today to about 400 acres, with about 3,300 employees by full buildout in 2045. Plans include a payload processing facility, a Starship test stand near Schwartz Road, a new four-lane road and buildings up to 400 feet tall; about 156 acres of wetlands would be affected. SpaceX vice president Kiko Dontchev said on 21 October that the pad 39A infrastructure is "effectively complete" and that after the Bandwagon-5 launch on 20 October "we have a six-week gap before the next Falcon 9," as SpaceX shifts its crews to Starship. The first Florida Starship launch may come by the end of the year.

items.headline: A pro-union historian says unionists can't refuse a second Scottish referendum forever, and proposes a third, confirming vote after any Yes
items.lead: Professor Colin Kidd of the University of St Andrews, who sits on the advisory council of the pro-union think tank These Islands, wrote in The Herald on 27 October that unionists "can't keep on saying no indefinitely" to a second referendum.
items.text: He proposed that any deal for a second vote include a third, binding referendum, either when independence talks conclude or ten years after independence, citing "buyer's remorse" after Brexit. He also warned that an independent Scotland taking on part of the UK's three trillion pounds of debt would face strict market discipline and "would almost certainly need to run a Thatcherite economic policy." Gordon MacIntyre-Kemp of the pro-independence Believe in Scotland criticized the idea in The Herald.

items.headline: Chi publishes an essay recounting a talk with Land: Land told her nature and grace "are the same under the sovereignty of God"
items.lead: @chithinksonline posted "Christian Hermetic Metaphysics: Agápē is Metamodern" on her Substack on 27 October, and @patallax promoted it on X as reading on "Network Spirituality."
items.text: In the essay she writes that when she spoke to Nick Land about Gnostic Calvinism and her own "Xenolutheranism," the talk came down to a disagreement over what nature is. In her account, Land told her that nature and grace are the same under the sovereignty of God, and that a miracle is not an exception to nature but one of its works beyond the reach of our judgment; Xenolutheranism, by contrast, negates nature to reach grace. This is her account only; Land has not posted about it. The same day she posted "A blessed guide to Xenolutheran eschatology" on X. Other watch-list activity since the last edition: Land posted only on politics and immigration; the Methexis Institute's Forbidden Books group meets 1 November on Christoph Schuringa's "A Social History of Analytic Philosophy," and Ryan Haecker posted his introduction to Walter Burley's "On the Purity of the Art of Logic" for the group; @AOElection posted on Original Sin and Total Depravity ("Original Sin = 189"); Net Void and CyphersNews posted only memes and reposts. Retrochronic is unchanged (v1.0.176, 199 sources), and no new Land video or podcast appeared.

items.headline: Jacques Vallée on the UAP Files Podcast: AI might contact the phenomenon "without us"
items.lead: On 24 October the UAP Files Podcast posted a 1 hour 51 minute conversation with Jacques Vallée, joined by Tom Vernon.
items.text: The episode asks whether artificial intelligence could make contact with non-human intelligence on its own; the description quotes Vallée: "The thing it could do on its own is to contact the phenomena, without us." It also covers crash retrievals and disclosure. On 19 October Ryan Sprague's Somewhere in the Skies posted a 1 hour 34 minute interview about his latest book, "Forbidden Science 7: The Final Report," his material analysis with Garry Nolan, and the Trinity crash case. His official site, jacquesvallee.net, has not changed. No link to Land or the CCRU was found.

items.headline: Backgrounder: the Arab vote, the Gaza war, and who the Arab parties are
items.lead: Arab turnout was a record, estimated at about 80 percent (Channel 12 estimate, not official). The Arab parties are four separate groups with different voters and ideas, and they work together only in part. The latest committee count we found, at 5:58 a.m. on 28 October, gave the Joint List and Ra'am 16 seats combined, against 18 or 19 in the exit polls.
items.text: Israel's Arab citizens voted in record numbers on 27 October. Channel 12 estimated Arab turnout at about 80 percent, which is an estimate and not an official figure. The Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) measured 53.2 percent in Arab and Druze towns in 2022. National turnout at the 10 p.m. close was 77.7 percent, up from 70.6 percent in 2022 (Times of Israel, citing the Central Elections Committee). That is the highest since 1999, when it was 78.7 percent (the committee's historical table; Times of Israel, Al Jazeera). Ynet wrote 'since 2001', but 2001 was a vote for prime minister only, at 62.3 percent, so we use 1999. The final Arab turnout is not yet published.
body: The count so far. The newest committee figures we could confirm are from 5:58 a.m. on 28 October, with 41.9 percent of ballot boxes counted: Joint List 12 seats, Ra'am 4, together 16. The Netanyahu bloc had 57 seats and the opposition 47 (Times of Israel). A seat tracker, israelielection.org, showed the same figures when checked at 7:15 a.m. (its seat counts are its own estimates). The final exit polls were Channel 13 at 1:14 a.m. (Joint List 11, Ra'am 7), Kan 11 at 1:40 a.m. (11 and 7) and Channel 12 at 2:17 a.m. (12 and 7), so 18 or 19 combined. Ra'am is below its exit-poll figure, and we found no confirmed reason. The count is partial, and double-envelope ballots, which include soldiers' votes, are counted later (Times of Israel). The two groups held 10 seats when the Knesset dissolved on 17 July: Hadash 3, Ta'al 2 and Ra'am 5 (israelielection.org).

The 2021 riots in mixed cities. These were in May 2021, not 2022, during the 11-day Gaza war. Arab and Jewish mobs fought in Lod, Acre, Jaffa, Haifa, Ramle, Tiberias and Bat Yam, and the worst eased by about 17 May (Times of Israel). The State Comptroller counted about 520 violent incidents, three civilians killed and hundreds hurt. They include Mousa Hassouna, an Arab man shot in Lod on 10 May by Jewish residents who said it was self-defense, and Yigal Yehoshua, a Jewish man hit by a brick in Lod on 11 May, who died on 17 May. A guest, Avi Har-Even, died after a Jewish-owned hotel in Acre was set on fire by Arab rioters. Synagogues in Lod were burned (Ynet counted eight; single source, unconfirmed). Police declared a state of emergency in Lod on 11-12 May and set an 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. curfew. Several Border Police companies were sent in, including a task force of about 500 officers (Jerusalem Post). About 3,200 people were arrested, about 240 of them Jews, and 574 were indicted (comptroller). We found no split of indictments by side. The US State Department gives a lower arrest figure, about 1,550, so the counts disagree. Prosecutors closed the case over Hassouna's death in October 2021, accepting self-defense; Adalah, an Arab rights group, alleges a flawed investigation, which is its claim and not a court finding.

Effect on relations and votes. In an IDI survey on 30-31 May 2021, about 36 percent of Israelis named Jewish-Arab tensions the main threat to Israel (37 percent of Jews, 30 percent of Arabs). IDI's April and August 2021 surveys found smaller changes than expected: Arabs felt less pride in being Israeli, and Jews were less willing to live alongside Arabs. Ra'am froze coalition talks on 10 May. Mansour Abbas condemned violence on both sides, said Arabs would repair the burned Lod synagogues, and visited one. Ra'am signed on 2 June, and the Bennett-Lapid government, the first with an independent Arab party, was sworn in on 13 June (BBC). In 2022, Arab turnout was 53.2 percent against 44.6 percent in March 2021, before the riots; Ra'am rose from four to five seats, and Balad led in Lod, Ramle and Jaffa (INSS). We found no study linking the riots to the 2022 or 2026 results, so that link is unconfirmed.

The Gaza war and Arab voters. Direct evidence is thin, so each item is attributed. In an IDI poll of 500 Arab citizens in December 2025, only 13 percent felt free to speak on social media, down from 21 percent in December 2023. A June 2025 Dayan Center survey found 75.2 percent said the war hurt Arab-Jewish relations, yet 54 percent named crime as the top issue and 23.2 percent named ending the war. In IDI's August-September 2026 poll, about 32 percent of Arab respondents (150 people, a small sample) called 7 October a central factor in their vote, against 68 percent of Jews. In September 2025, 93 percent of Arabs and 60 percent of Jews told IDI it is time to end the war. Police and prosecutions: Adalah, an Arab rights group, reported in October 2023 that the police commissioner refused permits for Gaza solidarity protests, that at least 80 people were arrested over social media posts and 17 at protests by 15 October, and that 89 students faced discipline. It says the Knesset ethics committee suspended Hadash lawmaker Ofer Cassif. In 2026 the Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify Cassif and Balad's Sami Abu Shehadeh. The Supreme Court reinstated Cassif 7 to 2. Abu Shehadeh withdrew on 2 October after the court's president said most justices favored barring him over an article that called 7 October 'an important historical event'; he denies supporting the attack (Al Jazeera). Bedouin: CNN reported in September 2024 that, per lawmaker Waleed Alhwashla, 22 Bedouin were killed on 7 October, 7 by rockets that hit unrecognized villages. The Hostage Families Forum counted 8 Bedouin kidnapped; as of that report three were freed, one was believed dead, one was killed by Israeli fire while fleeing and three were still held. That status is from 2024 and may be out of date. Turnout: Haaretz's Jack Khoury wrote that a right-wing scare campaign pushed Arab voters to the polls, and Al Jazeera's Nour Odeh said even habitual boycotters voted. We found no study that measures why. In the December 2025 IDI poll, 24 percent said they would not vote.

Who is who: Ra'am (United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas). Times of Israel calls it Islamist; J Street calls it the political arm of the Islamic Movement's southern branch. The Middle East Institute's Naif Abu Sharkia writes that the founder, Sheikh Abdullah Nimer Darwish, 'was part of the Muslim Brotherhood movement' but that the southern branch does not follow Brotherhood rulings as firmly as Hamas or the northern branch. So 'Brotherhood-aligned' fits its roots, not a current chain of command. Its base is Bedouin towns: in 2022 it won 73.9 percent of votes in the Negev (IDI). It joined the Bennett-Lapid government in 2021, the first Arab party in a coalition (IDI). This year it fields a Jewish candidate, Yoav Segalovitz, in second place (Al Jazeera; The Conversation).

Hadash (led by Yousef Jabareen, who replaced Ayman Odeh after winning 82 percent in a 16 May primary; Times of Israel). It is the Communist-rooted list, founded in 1977. IDI calls it far left and socialist, and it supports two states. It is an Arab-Jewish party with mostly Arab voters. In 2022 it led around Nazareth and the Sakhnin valley, with about 40 percent, and won some Jewish votes in mixed cities (IDI). Jabareen is from Umm al-Fahm, and Hadash is trying to win Triangle and Negev votes from Ra'am (Times of Israel).
Ta'al (led by Ahmad Tibi). Founded in 1996 by Tibi. IDI calls it secular, and J Street calls it Arab nationalist. It supports a Palestinian state and civil equality. It ran with Hadash in 2022.

Balad. Founded in 1996 by Azmi Bishara. IDI describes it as far left and secular, calling for 'a state of all its citizens', a Palestinian state with Jerusalem as capital and recognition of Arabs as a national minority. It was strongest in 2022 in the mixed central cities, Lod and Jaffa (IDI). It ran alone in 2022 and missed the threshold with 2.9 percent.

The northern branch of the Islamic Movement, led by Sheikh Raed Salah, is not on the ballot. Israel outlawed it on 17 November 2015 The government cited incitement and ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and Hamas (AP, in the Guardian). It rejects the Knesset; JFeed reported on 25 October that Salah and deputy Kamal Khatib urged a boycott and rejected both Ra'am's path and the Joint List's (single report, unconfirmed).

Who the voters are. About 2.1 million Arabs live in Israel, 20.9 percent of the population, which includes 3.7 percent who live in East Jerusalem. Arab citizens alone are 17.2 percent (end-2023 data from the Central Bureau of Statistics, in IDI's 2024 report). Of Arab citizens, 83.5 percent are Muslim (including about 300,000 Negev Bedouin, per CNN), 8.9 percent Druze and 7.6 percent Christian. A weaker secondary source gives 86.1, 6.8 and 7.1 for 2025, so treat these shares as approximate. About 49 percent live in the north, 19 percent in the Triangle, 18 percent in the Negev and 9 percent in mixed cities (IDI). Druze voters mostly choose Zionist parties: about 90 percent did so in 2022 (IDI). In some Galilee Christian villages Hadash-Ta'al finished first in 2022 with 39.8 percent (IDI).

Do they work together? Partly. The Joint List formed in 2015 after the electoral threshold was raised; it won 13 seats in 2015, broke apart before April 2019, ran again in September 2019 (13 seats) and 2020 (15 seats). Ra'am left before the 2021 vote, and in 2022 Balad also ran alone (IDI; Times of Israel). The differences are of ideology and government role. Ra'am wants to be in the government, including with Zionist parties. Hadash, Ta'al and Balad prefer to support or block from outside and oppose joining a government. They also differ on religion: Ra'am is conservative, the others secular or socialist. The four parties signed an agreement in January, reported by J Street as 22 January in Sakhnin, to revive the list (Times of Israel). Talks then stalled because Abbas wanted a purely technical list, and the other three would not promise to avoid opposing any government Ra'am joined (Times of Israel, 10 June). Hadash, Ta'al and Balad went ahead without Ra'am. The two sides signed a surplus-vote agreement in September, under which leftover votes are pooled, with a pledge of a clean campaign (Ynetnews). The Official Gazette published it on 19 October (israelielection.org, one source).

What they say now. Jabareen: 'we will make the responsible decision... that will ultimately send Netanyahu home.' Tibi: 'Without the Joint List, it's impossible to tip the balance.' and 'After the election, we'll get a phone call' (+972 Magazine, 27 October). The Conversation reports that the Joint List offered outside support on conditions, including a funded crime plan, and that Abbas and Jabareen condemned 7 October. The rivalry is open: a Joint List official, Noa Levy, criticized Ra'am for not raising the occupation (+972). On 28 October Abbas said the opposition must reach 61 seats and that 'with the numbers we have now, there is no government' (Al Jazeera). Gadi Eisenkot said Ra'am, 'including Mansour Abbas', would not be in his government; Segalovitz replied that Eisenkot cannot form one without Ra'am (Times of Israel, 26 September).

Unconfirmed or in dispute. Final seats and Arab turnout; why Ra'am trails its exit polls; the 2024 hostage status of the Bedouin; the JFeed boycott report; the Gazette date. We did not find Arab-sector polling that asks directly how the Gaza war changed party choice.
